title: --acceptance-criteria silently clears every checked box when given a string array, and the object form that preserves them is documented only in a usage error
description:
Found 2026-09-15 while amending one acceptance criterion on QCLI-307, by measuring rather than by reading the code.

`quest task edit <id> --acceptance-criteria` accepts EITHER a JSON array of strings OR an array of `{index,text,checked}` objects. The object form preserves checked state and is the only way to amend one criterion's text without losing the others. The string form silently clears every box.

MEASURED in a throwaway workspace, three criteria with positions 1 and 3 checked:

  string array, one text amended       both checked items SILENTLY reset to false,
                                       envelope returns kind=task.updated, no warning
  objects without `index`              exit 2 usage: "--acceptance-criteria must be a
                                       JSON array of strings or {index,text,checked} items."
  objects with {index,text,checked}    one text amended, both checked states preserved

TWO DEFECTS, and they compound:

1. DISCOVERABILITY. The object form appears in exactly one place in the CLI's own output -- the usage error above. `quest manifest --json` describes the flag as `{"value":"json-array"}` and nothing more. `quest help task edit`'s summary explains --check-ac/--uncheck-ac/--remove-ac and the 1-based position vs 0-based index distinction at length and never mentions that --acceptance-criteria takes objects. So an agent reading the manifest -- which is what `quest instructions overview` tells it to read for the command contract -- concludes the flag takes strings, and is wrong.

2. SILENT DESTRUCTION. The string form is a reasonable thing to reach for and it destroys state with no signal. A caller who does not read the record back cannot tell. This is worse than the discoverability gap on its own, because the two combine into: the documented-looking path silently loses data, and the safe path is documented only on the failure branch.

WHY THIS IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN DOCUMENTING. This repository's own CLAUDE.md warns against inferring a fact from a neighbouring one instead of measuring it. The session that found this had recorded that warning in a tracker note in the same hour, then read `"value":"json-array"`, inferred "array of strings", and wrote the inference into a task note as though it were measured -- caught only by probing the flag before filing. A warning did not prevent it; a manifest that named the shape would have.

Not urgent: no data is known to have been lost, and QCLI-307's own amendment was made correctly with the object form. Filing so the next caller does not have to discover it the same way.

acceptanceCriteria.text: quest manifest --json describes --acceptance-criteria (and --definition-of-done, which shares the shape) in a form a caller can act on without triggering a usage error first -- the object alternative is discoverable from the machine contract, not only from the failure path
quest help task edit names the {index,text,checked} form in its prose, alongside the existing position-vs-index explanation

The string form no longer silently clears checked state: it either preserves it by matching on position, or it is refused with a message naming the object form -- decided deliberately and recorded, not left to whichever is easier

Proven both ways as two separate runs: a string-array edit behaves as decided, and an object-array edit amends one entry with every other checked state preserved, each verified by reading the record back rather than by the command's exit code

implementationNotes:
SECOND INDEPENDENT INSTANCE, SAME EVENING, DIFFERENT REPOSITORY. This raises the severity and it changes the diagnosis.

opum-agent reported 2026-09-15 23:40Z that it used the string form of --acceptance-criteria that same night, on OPAG-148, to add a fifth criterion to one of its own tasks. It did not know the object form existed and states it would have had no way to find out. It escaped loss only because all five criteria happened to be unchecked at the time -- it read the record back to confirm: 5 criteria, 0 checked, nothing lost. Its own word for that is luck, not care.

So within a few hours, two sessions in two repositories independently reached for the same lossy form, neither knowing the lossless one existed. ONE CALLER REACHING FOR THE DESTRUCTIVE PATH IS A CALLER MISTAKE; TWO INDEPENDENT CALLERS REACHING FOR IT IS THE DISCOVERABLE PATH BEING THE DESTRUCTIVE ONE. The string form is what the machine contract advertises, and it is the one that destroys state.

WHAT THIS CHANGES IN THE FIX, and it is not just a priority bump. The third criterion offers a choice -- preserve checked state by position, or refuse the string form with a message naming the object form -- and this instance argues against leaving that open much longer, because BOTH observed callers were agents reading `quest manifest --json` to learn the contract. An agent cannot be told to prefer the object form by a convention it never reads. The manifest criterion is therefore the load-bearing one; the help-text criterion is for humans and is secondary to it.

IT ALSO NARROWS THE BLAST RADIUS QUESTION. Two instances, zero actual losses, both by the same accident: the criteria involved were unchecked. That is worth stating precisely rather than dramatising -- the flag has not been shown to have lost data, only to be unable to signal when it does. The severity is in the silence and the advertising, not in a known loss.

Not folded into this task's description, which records the original discovery as it happened. A second instance reported by a third party belongs in the notes with its date and its source.

--definition-of-done MEASURED, no longer inferred. Criterion 1 named it as "which shares the shape" and that was an inference; the first note in this task hedged it correctly as "I have not probed it separately, so treat that as inferred, not measured", and then the criterion asserted it anyway. Same session, same hour, and the assertion is the one that would have been read as fact.

Caught by opum-cli-e2e, who noticed they were about to relay the inferred claim onward as confirmed and declined -- then pointed out that the criterion had already done what they had just refused to do. The relay was stopped one hop downstream; the hardened version was already upstream of it.

MEASURED in a throwaway workspace, three items with positions 1 and 3 checked:
  string array, one text amended       both checked items SILENTLY reset to false
  objects with {index,text,checked}    one text amended, both checked states preserved
Identical to --acceptance-criteria in both directions. Criterion 1 now rests on a measurement.

TWO THINGS FROM opum-cli-e2e WORTH KEEPING.

1. The manifest fix alone does not close this, and their reason is better than my criterion's. `{"value":"json-array"}` becoming `{"value":"json-array<{index,text,checked}>"}` fixes the SHAPE and says nothing about the destructive semantics of the other accepted form. A caller reading the improved manifest learns the object form exists; they do not learn the string form drops state. So a better manifest makes the trap RARER WITHOUT MAKING IT VISIBLE, and rarer-but-silent is the profile that produces the long-lived defect. Criterion 3 already asks for the refuse-or-preserve decision to be made deliberately; this argues specifically for REFUSE, because a silent preserve still never tells the caller what they nearly did.

2. They separated two candidate tests that I had collapsed into one. A RECORDS row edits one criterion's text and asserts the others' checked states survived -- the regression test for this task. A CONTRACT row asserts that a mutating command's success envelope can express what it did, because `kind=task.updated` plus exit 0 is emitted identically for a lossless and a lossy edit. The second is the bigger claim and recurs independently of this flag. They have not filed either yet, deliberately, having four open records from tonight already; they will route the id.

They also confirmed the object form from the consumer side incidentally rather than deliberately -- their TASK-74 edit preserved all three checked states, verified by re-reading the record rather than trusting the envelope -- and reported they had been about to pass a string array, on the same reasoning: the manifest says json-array and `quest help task edit` never mentions the object form. That is a THIRD independent caller reaching for the lossy form, after this session and opum-agent.
